ANALYTIC FRAMEWORK
The social and economic impact assessment process depends on an assumed set of relationships among important demographic and economic variables in the area under investigation. The assumed set of relationships is often referred to as a model; and, because much of what comes out of the analysis is a direct consequence of the assumed structure of the model, it is important that the economic-demographic simulation model used in this study be briefly explained and that the critical assumptions on which it is based be identified. 1/
A. THE ECONOMIC-DEMOGRAPHIC SIMULATION MODEL
The economic-demographic simulation model provides a framework within which the interaction of the demographic structure and the economic base of the Impact Area can be studied. The five components of the model and the purposes they serve are as follows:
Demographic Submodel—This submodel starts with the base population of the Impact Area, survives it, and allows babies to be born. The new population then joins the labor force based on an assumed set of age-race-sex specific labor force participation rates. The two outputs of this submodel are population and labor force.
Economic Submodel--The economic submodel begins with basic employment and population and generates estimates of total employment by industry.
Racial Allocation of Employment Submodel—The available Crow labor force is compared to the total number of jobs assumed to be available to the Crows. The proportion of new jobs in any given industry that will be available to the Crows is referred to as the Crow "entry factor" and was estimated to reflect both the historical level of participation of Crows
Substantially more information on the technical details of the model are contained in the Baseline Report, pp. 5-114, and in the Technical Report, pp. 1-146.
